**Rivers**

A river begins quietly. Somewhere high up, rain gathers in a fold of rock, or snow melts into a trickle that would fit in a cupped hand. That trickle finds another, and another, and before long the water has a direction and a name. From there it does the same thing every river has done since water first moved across land: it goes downhill, and it takes the shortest path it can find.

That path is rarely straight. Rivers meander, swinging wide across their floodplains in great looping curves. The outside of each bend erodes while the inside builds up sediment, so the curves grow more exaggerated over centuries until the river finally cuts through its own neck and leaves an oxbow lake behind. A river is never finished. It is always rewriting its own course.

People have always settled beside rivers. They offer drinking water, fish, irrigation, transport, and power. The Nile made Egypt possible. The Tigris and Euphrates cradled the first cities. The Mississippi carried the commerce of a young nation, and the Yangtze still moves more freight than almost any waterway on Earth. Cities grow where rivers can be crossed or where they meet the sea.

Rivers also carry what we discard. Silt, fertilizer, plastic, and industrial runoff all travel downstream, which is why a river's health reflects everything that happens across its whole basin. Restoring one means restoring the land around it.

Yet rivers are resilient. Remove a dam and salmon return within a few seasons. Replant a bank and the water clears. A river wants to be a river, and given even a little room, it will find its way back to the sea.
